title: The Aral Sea
sources: Every claim is checked against episodes/aral-sea/research.md (R1-R7) and episodes/aral-sea/factcheck.md.
Own measurement R1 (tools/aral_numbers.py, Landsat NDWI > 0.05 inside the Natural Earth 1960s outline): summer 2026 4797 km2 (7.1 % of 67190 km2); North Aral 2002 2882 km2 -> 2026 2888 km2.

youtube.title: The Aral Sea Shrank 93%. Then One Part Came Back
youtube.description:
In 1960 the Aral Sea was the fourth-largest lake on Earth. We measured what is left on Landsat images from the summer of 2026, inside the 1960s shoreline. How Soviet cotton drained it, the anthrax island it exposed, the dust desert it left behind, the dam that brought the northern half back, and the new canal in Afghanistan that may take more of its river.

Real NASA MODIS, Landsat and Copernicus Sentinel-2 images, astronaut photographs and our own measurements.
youtube.pinned_comment: Should Afghanistan be free to take Amu Darya water for its farms, even if the countries downstream lose some of theirs?

paragraphs.text: This is the Aral Sea in August 2000, seen by a NASA satellite. Now watch the same place in August 2026.
Most of what just disappeared was water. It is now a desert with its own name, the Aralkum.
And in 1960, the sea was bigger still. This was its shoreline, about 68,000 square kilometres.

stat.label: the Aral Sea in 1960
stat.source: Published figure; outline from Natural Earth

paragraphs.text: That made it the fourth-largest lake on Earth, a little bigger than Sri Lanka.

stat.label: largest lake on Earth in 1960

shots.on_screen_text: The Aral Sea from space, August 1964

paragraphs.text: We measured what is left on Landsat images from this summer. Inside the old shoreline, we found about 4,800 square kilometres of open water.

stat.label: of open water inside the 1960s shoreline, summer 2026

paragraphs.text: That is about 7 percent of the sea that was here in 1960.

chart.title: Aral Sea water area
chart.source: Natural Earth 1960s outline; our Landsat measurement

paragraphs.text: And yet one part of it is coming back. In the north, the water rose by about twelve metres after 2003.

stat.label: rise of the North Aral's level, 2003 to 2008

paragraphs.text: And the fish returned.

shots.on_screen_text: The North Aral from the International Space Station, May 2022

paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, far to the south, a new canal in Afghanistan is about to start drawing water.
It draws from the river that once fed most of this sea.
So who should get a river's water: the farms along it, or the sea at its end?

shots.on_screen_text: The Aral Sea from the Space Shuttle, 1997

ask.text: A river's water: for the farms, or for the sea?

paragraphs.text: Here is how a sea that size disappeared, and how part of it came back.
Start in Muynak, in western Uzbekistan.
In the 1960s it was a fishing port, with a cannery and boats on the water.
Today its boats rest on sand. The water is now around a hundred kilometres away.

stat.label: from Muynak to the water today

paragraphs.text: Across the whole sea, fishing once employed about forty thousand people.

shots.on_screen_text: A stranded ship on the old seabed, 2005

stat.label: people in the Aral's fishing industry at its peak

paragraphs.text: The Aral was reported to supply a sixth of all the fish caught in the Soviet Union.

stat.label: of the Soviet Union's fish catch came from the Aral, reportedly

paragraphs.text: By 1987, commercial fishing here had stopped.

stat.label: commercial fishing ends

paragraphs.text: Muynak's cannery kept going for a while anyway, on frozen fish brought in from the Baltic Sea.

shots.on_screen_text: Fish from the Baltic, by rail and truck

paragraphs.text: That was more than three thousand kilometres away, by rail and truck.

stat.label: from the Baltic to Muynak's cannery

paragraphs.text: When the Soviet Union broke up, the shipments stopped.
In 1993, the cannery made four million cans. It was built for twenty-seven million.
Even the muskrats went. Trappers in the river deltas once took up to half a million pelts a year.

stat.label: muskrat pelts a year, at the peak

paragraphs.text: Up in the north, the Kazakh port of Aralsk lost its sea too.
At its worst, the shoreline was reported to be about a hundred kilometres from the town.

stat.label: from Aralsk to the shore at the worst, reportedly
stat.note: Other reports give about 40 km in 2005

paragraphs.text: Ships were left where the water had been.
So where did all that water go? It was sent somewhere on purpose, to grow one crop.
Two rivers feed the Aral. The Amu Darya comes down from the Pamir mountains in the south.
The Syr Darya comes from the Tien Shan, in the east.
The Amu Darya once brought about seventy percent of the sea's water.

stat.label: of the Aral's water came from the Amu Darya

paragraphs.text: In the 1960s, Soviet planners turned both rivers into irrigation water for cotton and other crops.

shots.on_screen_text: The Aral Sea from the Space Shuttle, April 1994

paragraphs.text: The fields spread across what are now Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.
One canal, the Karakum, carries Amu Darya water hundreds of kilometres across the Turkmen desert.
A large share of its water never reaches a field.

stat.label: of the Karakum Canal's water lost on the way, estimates say

paragraphs.text: It leaks into the sand or evaporates on the way.
With less water arriving, the sea began to fall, about twenty centimetres a year in the 1960s.

stat.label: a year: the fall in the 1960s

paragraphs.text: By the 1980s it was dropping eighty to ninety centimetres every year.

stat.label: a year: the fall in the 1980s

paragraphs.text: The water that stayed behind grew saltier.
By 1990 it was nearly as salty as the ocean.

stat.label: salt in the Aral by 1990

paragraphs.text: In 1987, the sea broke in two. A small northern sea stayed in Kazakhstan.
A large southern sea was shared with Uzbekistan.
We measured how fast it went. In the summer of 1989, Landsat shows about 40,500 square kilometres of water.

stat.label: of water inside the 1960s shoreline, summer 1989

paragraphs.text: By the summer of 2002, it was down to about 22,000.

chart.title: Aral Sea water area
chart.source: Natural Earth 1960s outline; our Landsat measurements

paragraphs.text: Between 1960 and 1998, the Aral lost about sixty percent of its area, and eighty percent of its water.

stat.label: of the area lost, 1960 to 1998
of the water lost, 1960 to 1998

paragraphs.text: By the 1970s, the sea's decline was impossible to miss. Moscow's answer was bigger still.

shots.on_screen_text: The Aral Sea from the Space Shuttle, 1994

paragraphs.text: The plan was to turn some of Siberia's rivers around, and send their water south.
In 1976, a Communist Party congress approved it.

stat.label: the Party congress approves the river plan

paragraphs.text: One version would have moved up to forty cubic kilometres of water a year toward Central Asia.

stat.label: a year southward, in one version of the plan

paragraphs.text: Ten years later, in August 1986, the plan was dropped, over its cost and strong opposition.

stat.label: the river plan is cancelled

paragraphs.text: Siberian communities and scientists had fought it. Almost nothing had been built.
Some Central Asian officials still talk about reviving the idea. Russian officials have said they have no such plans.
So nothing came to refill the Aral. And as the water drew back, it uncovered something the Soviet Union had kept secret.

shots.on_screen_text: The Aral Sea from the Space Shuttle, September 2000

paragraphs.text: In the middle of the sea lay an island called Vozrozhdeniya. The name means rebirth.
When a Russian naval expedition first surveyed the sea, in 1848 and 1849, the island was named after Tsar Nicholas the First.

shots.photo: File:1848 09 13 (circa) - Shevchenko, Butakov and others on the shore of the Nicholas I Island (Vozrozhdeniya).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: On the island, 1848: drawing by Taras Shevchenko

paragraphs.text: The Ukrainian poet Taras Shevchenko sailed with that expedition as its artist.

stat.label: Butakov's expedition: the first survey of the Aral
stat.source: Taras Shevchenko Museum; Russian Geographical Society records

paragraphs.text: For decades, the Soviet military used it as an open-air test site for biological weapons.

shots.photo: File:Aral Sea, Vozrozhdeniya Island and Komsomolsky, Konstantin, Bellinsgauzena, Lazareva islands, LandSat-1 satellite image, 20-SEP-1972.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Vozrozhdeniya and its neighbours, Landsat 1, September 1972

paragraphs.text: In 1988, anthrax was buried there.

stat.label: anthrax buried on the island

paragraphs.text: Estimates of the amount range from a hundred to two hundred tonnes.

stat.label: of anthrax, by different estimates

paragraphs.text: Then the island stopped being an island. Around 2001, the shrinking sea joined it to the mainland.

stat.label: the island joins the mainland

paragraphs.text: The United States paid for a cleanup.
Teams dug up eleven burial pits and decontaminated them.

stat.label: of buried anthrax dug up and decontaminated

paragraphs.text: Kantubek, the island's small town, was left empty.
The bigger danger from the old seabed lies on its surface, and the wind carries it.
In the summer of 2014, NASA reported that the eastern basin of the southern sea had dried up completely.
It was the first time in modern history.

stat.label: the eastern basin dries up completely

paragraphs.text: In wet years some water has spread back over it for a while. On our August 2026 image, it is dry.

shots.on_screen_text: The southern tip of the South Aral, August 2025

paragraphs.text: What is left is a plain of salt, which researchers say is mixed with residue from decades of cotton farming.

shots.on_screen_text: Salt flats on the old seabed

paragraphs.text: That farming used heavy doses of pesticide and fertiliser.

shots.on_screen_text: The old seabed near Barsakelmes, August 2024

paragraphs.text: Storms lift tens of millions of tonnes of salt, sand and dust off the seabed every year.

stat.label: of tonnes of salt and dust blown off the seabed each year
stat.note: Sources give 80 to over 100 million t
stat.source: Global Voices; Times of Central Asia

paragraphs.text: Researchers have linked the crisis to poor health around the sea. One study found that a quarter of the children were born underweight.

stat.label: of children in the region born with low birth weight

paragraphs.text: One study put child mortality in the region at seventy-five per thousand births in 2009.

stat.label: child mortality in the Aral region, 2009

paragraphs.text: Studies count at least four point four million people affected around the sea.

stat.label: people affected by the crisis, at least

paragraphs.text: Losing the water changed the weather too.
Without a big lake to soften it, the region's winters became colder and its summers hotter.

stat.label: winters, and hotter summers, after the sea shrank

paragraphs.text: For years the Aral was taught as a lost cause. Then, in 2005, Kazakhstan finished a wall across it.
This is the Kokaral dam, a thirteen-kilometre wall of earth.

stat.label: of dam across the old channel

paragraphs.text: It runs across the channel where the northern sea used to drain south.
It cost about eighty-six million dollars, much of it lent by the World Bank.

stat.label: for the dam and river works
stat.note: Including a $64.5 million World Bank loan

paragraphs.text: It was finished in August 2005.

stat.label: the dam is finished

paragraphs.text: The idea was simple: keep the Syr Darya's water in the north, where it could fill a smaller sea.
It filled faster than expected, within about a year, according to the World Bank.

stat.label: for the North Aral to fill behind the dam

paragraphs.text: Most of the change was in depth. The sea rose behind the dam, and the water freshened.
We measured the northern sea on this summer's Landsat images: about 2,900 square kilometres.

stat.label: the North Aral, summer 2026

paragraphs.text: That is close to Kazakhstan's own figure of 3,065 square kilometres, for February 2025.
By 2008 its level stood twelve metres higher than in 2003.

stat.label: North Aral level, 2003 to 2008

paragraphs.text: And the water became far less salty, from about thirty grams of salt per litre to eight.

stat.label: salt in the North Aral before and after the dam

paragraphs.text: The fish came back. In 2004, the catch here was fifty-two tonnes.

stat.label: of fish caught in the North Aral in 2004

paragraphs.text: In recent years it has been around eight thousand tonnes a year.

stat.label: of fish a year in recent years
stat.source: Times of Central Asia; Global Voices

paragraphs.text: Twenty-two species have returned.

shots.on_screen_text: The North Aral from the ISS, May 2022

paragraphs.text: The shore has moved back toward Aralsk too. It is now about twenty-five kilometres from the town.

stat.label: from Aralsk to the shore now

paragraphs.text: In 2012, the northern sea and the Syr Darya delta were listed as wetlands of international importance.

stat.label: the North Aral and the Syr Darya delta become a Ramsar site

paragraphs.text: Kazakhstan's ministry says the northern sea held 23.4 billion cubic metres of water in August 2026.
More than six billion cubic metres have flowed in over the past three years.
To send more water downstream, it now pays farmers up to eighty percent of the cost of water-saving equipment.

stat.label: of water-saving equipment paid for farmers

paragraphs.text: There is a cost. The dam keeps the northern water in the north.
That also cut off the flow that used to reach the southern sea.
And the fishing boom is not guaranteed. In 2025, the catch was reported to have halved.
We measure places like this from orbit in every episode, so if you want to see where we look next, subscribe.
Kazakhstan saved the part it could. Was that the right call, or should the whole sea have been the goal?

ask.text: Save the part you can, or fight for the whole sea?

paragraphs.text: Now Kazakhstan wants more. A second phase, planned for 2026 to 2029, would raise the dam.
It would lift the sea to forty-four metres above sea level, and grow it to about 3,900 square kilometres.

stat.label: the level the second phase aims for
stat.source: Kazakhstan's water ministry, via Astana Times

stat.label: the area planned after the second phase
stat.source: Kazakhstan's water ministry, via Astana Times

paragraphs.text: That depends on the money being approved.
Kazakhstan's water minister has called the project a social and strategic task for all of Central Asia.
On the Uzbek side, the big effort is on the dry seabed itself.
Uzbekistan's government says it has planted protective forests on two million hectares since 2018.

stat.label: of the dry seabed planted, 2018 to 2025, Uzbekistan says

paragraphs.text: One of the main plants is saxaul, a tough desert shrub that can live on salty ground.
Kazakhstan reports about one point one million hectares planted on its side.

stat.label: planted on the Kazakh side, 2021 to 2025

paragraphs.text: The idea is to hold down the salt and dust with roots before the wind takes it.
On the ground, the results are uneven.
A 2025 report found one planting where more than half the trees had survived. At other sites, almost none had.

stat.label: survival of the seabed plantings
stat.note: Over half alive at one site, almost none at others

paragraphs.text: Experts quoted in that reporting argue that one species alone will not be enough, and suggest mixing plants.
What remains of the southern sea is the long western basin.
Its water is now too salty for the fish that once lived there.
But one tiny animal thrives in it: the brine shrimp.

stat.label: thrive in the salty western basin

paragraphs.text: It was first found here in 1998, probably carried in by migrating birds.

stat.label: brine shrimp first found in the Uzbek Aral

paragraphs.text: Since 2010, its eggs have been harvested commercially.

stat.label: first big commercial harvest of brine shrimp eggs

paragraphs.text: Workers spend the winter in small cabins on the shore, in temperatures that can fall to minus forty.

stat.label: winter temperatures for the harvesters

paragraphs.text: A biologist told Dialogue Earth it may be only a matter of years before the Uzbek side is too salty even for them.
Uzbekistan is also moving toward oil exploration on the drying seabed.
Now follow the Amu Darya upstream, all the way to Uzbekistan's border with Afghanistan.
This is the desert near the border in the summer of 2021. And this is the same place in July 2026.
That line is the Qosh Tepa canal. Afghanistan began building it in 2022, to take water from the Amu Darya.
It went fast. Planet Labs satellite images showed more than a hundred kilometres dug between April 2022 and February 2023.

stat.label: of canal dug between April 2022 and February 2023

paragraphs.text: The first phase was finished in October 2023.

stat.label: phase one of the canal finished

paragraphs.text: It is planned to run two hundred and eighty-five kilometres.

stat.label: the planned length of the canal

paragraphs.text: The goal is to turn five hundred and fifty thousand hectares of desert into farmland.

stat.label: of new farmland planned in northern Afghanistan

paragraphs.text: In March 2026, Afghan officials said the second phase was ninety-eight percent complete.

stat.label: of phase two complete, Afghan officials said in March 2026

paragraphs.text: The whole canal is expected to be finished by the end of this year.
How much water will it take? Estimates vary. The most cited range is six to ten cubic kilometres a year.

stat.label: a year: the most cited estimate of what the canal may take

paragraphs.text: That is roughly a fifth to a quarter of the river's average flow.

stat.label: of the Amu Darya's average flow
stat.note: Estimates vary with the baseline used

paragraphs.text: Uzbekistan has said it is worried about its farms downstream.
Environmental experts warn the canal could make the Aral's situation worse.
Afghanistan's Taliban government says the country has the right to use the river.
It says it is only taking its fair share.
Look at this patch of water beside the canal.
In December 2023, satellite images showed water spreading about nine kilometres along its northern bank.

stat.label: of water along the canal bank, December 2023

paragraphs.text: Afghan officials denied the canal had breached, and said the water had been sent there on purpose.
Back to the whole sea. Here is the shoreline of 1960.
And here is the water this summer: about 4,800 square kilometres.
From about 40,500 in 1989, to 22,000 in 2002, to 4,800 now.
In the north, a dam brought the water back, metre by metre.
In the south, people are planting forests where boats used to sail.
And upstream, a new canal is about to start taking its share of the river.
So should Afghanistan be free to take Amu Darya water for its farms, even if the countries downstream lose some of theirs?

ask.text: Should Afghanistan take Amu Darya water for its farms?
